replacement: In the United States the majority undertakes to supply individuals with a multitude of ready-made opinions, and so relieves them of the need to form opinions of their own. Everyone there adopts great numbers of theories on philosophy, morals, and politics without inquiry, on public trust. And if we look very closely, we will see that religion herself holds sway there much less as a doctrine of revelation than as a commonly received opinion. The political laws of the Americans give the majority sovereign rule over the community, and this materially increases the power the majority naturally exercises over the mind. For nothing is more common in man than to recognize superior wisdom in the person of his oppressor. This political omnipotence of the majority in the United States undoubtedly increases the influence that public opinion would have over each member of the community even without it. But the foundations of that influence do not rest on it. They must be sought in the principle of equality itself, not in the more or less popular institutions that people living under that condition may give themselves. The intellectual dominion of the greater number would probably be less absolute among a democratic people governed by a king than in a pure democracy, but it will always be extremely absolute. And whatever political laws govern people in the ages of equality, we can foresee that faith in public opinion will become a kind of religion there, with the majority as its ministering prophet.

replacement: The Americans are much more given to the use of general ideas than the English, and have a much greater taste for them. At first sight this seems very strange, when we remember that the two nations have the same origin, that they lived for centuries under the same laws, and that they still constantly exchange their opinions and their customs. The contrast becomes much more striking if we look at our own part of the world and compare the two most educated nations that live in it. The English mind seems able to tear itself away from the observation of particular facts, and rise from them to their causes, only reluctantly and painfully. It seems to generalize only in spite of itself. Among the French, on the contrary, the taste for general ideas seems to have grown into so ardent a passion that it must be satisfied on every occasion. Every morning when I wake I am told that some general and eternal law has just been discovered, one I had never heard mentioned before. There is not a mediocre scribbler who does not try his hand at discovering truths that apply to a great kingdom, and who is not very displeased with himself if he fails to squeeze the human race into the space of an article. It surprises me that two very educated nations should differ so much. If I turn my attention back to England and look at the events there over the last half-century, I think I can affirm that the taste for general ideas grows in that country in proportion as its ancient constitution weakens.
